name: Alioramus
dietDetails: Carnivorous predator preying on small-to-medium dinosaurs, oviraptorosaurs, and juvenile ornithischians.
sizeNotes: Based on subadult holotype PIN 3141/1, characterized by a slender gracile build and elongated skull.
discoveryHistory: Discovered by a Soviet-Mongolian paleontological expedition in the Gobi Desert in the early 1970s and formally described by Sergei Kurzanov in 1976.
interestingFacts: Distinguished by a prominent row of five bony crests or bumps along the bridge of its slender snout.
Possessed more teeth than any other tyrannosaurid (76 to 78 teeth), adapted for seizing smaller, agile prey.
Its slender proportions led researchers to suggest it occupied a distinct ecological niche compared to apex Tarbosaurus.
Histological analysis of Alioramus altai showed that even near-adult individuals maintained a long, gracile snout.

sources.citation: Kurzanov, S. M. (1976). A new late Cretaceous carnosaur from Nogon-Tsav, Mongolia. Trudy Sovmestnaya Sovetsko-Mongol'skaya Paleontologicheskaya Ekspeditsiya.
Brusatte, S. L., Carr, T. D., Erickson, G. M., Bever, G. S., & Norell, M. A. (2009). A long-snouted, multi-horned tyrannosaurid from the Late Cretaceous of Mongolia. PNAS, 106(41), 17261-17266.

name: Saurornitholestes
dietDetails: Active carnivore preying on small mammals, lizards, frogs, and juvenile dinosaurs; also scavenged larger carcasses.
sizeNotes: Lightly built dromaeosaurid with exceptionally long, slender hindlimbs and large sickle claws on the second toes.
discoveryHistory: Discovered by Wann Langston Jr. in 1974 at Dinosaur Provincial Park, Alberta, and formally named by Hans-Dieter Sues in 1978.
interestingFacts: One of the most abundant small theropods discovered in the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta.
A partial pterosaur bone (azhdarchid wing bone) was discovered with embedded Saurornitholestes teeth, indicating scavenging behavior.
Possessed specialized olfactory bulbs in the brain, suggesting a sharp sense of smell for tracking nocturnal prey.
Featured unusually large sickle claws relative to its body size compared to contemporary velociraptorines.

sources.citation: Sues, H.-D. (1978). A new small theropod dinosaur from the Judith River Formation of Alberta, Canada. Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society, 62(4), 381-400.
Currie, P. J., & Evans, D. C. (2019). Cranial anatomy of new specimens of Saurornitholestes langstoni and palaeoecology of Alberta dromaeosaurids. The Anatomical Record, 303(4), 690-715.

name: Deinocheirus
dietDetails: Bulk omnivore feeding on soft aquatic vegetation, water plants, freshwater fish, and small aquatic invertebrates.
sizeNotes: The largest known ornithomimosaurian, sporting massive 2.4-meter arms ending in blunt, curved 20-centimeter claws.
discoveryHistory: First discovered in 1965 by Zofia Kielan-Jaworowska as giant mysterious arms; its bizarre complete body with duck-bill and dorsal sail was revealed in 2014 by Lee et al.
interestingFacts: Remained one of paleontology's greatest mysteries for nearly 50 years when only its gargantuan arms were known.
Featured a prominent sail-like hump along its back supported by tall neural spines and a fused pygostyle at the tail tip.
Fossilized stomach contents revealed fish scales alongside over 1,400 gastroliths used to grind tough plant matter.
Possessed a wide, toothless, duck-like bill ideal for scooping aquatic vegetation in Cretaceous wetlands.

sources.citation: Lee, Y. N., Barsbold, R., Currie, P. J., et al. (2014). Resolving the long-standing enigmas of a giant ornithomimosaur Deinocheirus mirificus. Nature, 515(7526), 257-260.

name: Erlikosaurus
dietDetails: Herbivore consuming foliage, ferns, fruits, and soft Cretaceous vegetation.
sizeNotes: Known from the only exceptionally preserved complete skull of any therizinosaurid found to date (holotype MPC-D 100/111).
discoveryHistory: Found during a Soviet-Mongolian expedition in 1972 at Bayshin Tsav and formally named by Altangerel Perle in 1980.
interestingFacts: Provides the primary anatomical blueprint for the entire Therizinosauridae group thanks to its intact 25-centimeter skull.
Possessed a keratinous beak at the tip of its snout accompanied by small, leaf-shaped serrated teeth for stripping leaves.
Digital endocranial reconstructions revealed well-developed sense organs for hearing, balance, and spatial coordination.
Had slender, curved claws on its forelimbs used to hook high branches and pull foliage toward its mouth.

sources.citation: Perle, A. (1980). Segnosauria - a new infraorder of carnivorous dinosaurs. Trudy Sovmestnaya Sovetsko-Mongol'skaya Paleontologicheskaya Ekspeditsiya, 15, 87-103.
Lautenschlager, S., Rayfield, E. J., Altangerel, P., Zanno, L. E., & Witmer, L. M. (2012). The cranial paleoneurology of Erlikosaurus andrewsi. PLoS ONE, 7(12), e52289.

name: Mastodonsaurus
dietDetails: Ambush predator hunting freshwater fish, temnospondyls, and small terrestrial archosaurs entering shallow waterways.
sizeNotes: One of the largest amphibians to ever exist, with a massive triangular skull reaching up to 1.4 meters in length.
discoveryHistory: First described by Georg Friedrich von Jäger in 1828 based on a distinctive tooth cusp; complete massive skeletons were later uncovered in southern Germany.
interestingFacts: Possessed two enormous upward-pointing tusks on the lower jaw that poked completely through openings in the upper snout when the mouth closed.
Its reduced limbs and flattened aquatic body meant it lived almost entirely submerged in water.
Multiple fossil bonebeds show hundreds of individuals perished together in shrinking drought ponds during seasonal dry spells.
Lateral line sensory grooves along its skull allowed it to detect pressure waves generated by swimming prey.

sources.citation: Schoch, R. R. (1999). Comparative osteology of Mastodonsaurus giganteus (Jaeger, 1828) from the Middle Triassic of Germany. Stuttgarter Beiträge zur Naturkunde Serie B, 278, 1-175.

name: Asian Straight-tusked Elephant
dietDetails: Megaherbivore grazing on grasses and browsing on trees, shrubs, and bamboo across Indian river valleys.
sizeNotes: Often cited as the largest land mammal of the Quaternary period, with shoulder heights reaching up to 4.5 meters and estimated weights up to 15-22 tonnes.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in 1834 by Hugh Falconer and Proby Cautley in the Narmada Valley of Madhya Pradesh, India, and described in 1845.
interestingFacts: Considered by many paleontologists as the largest terrestrial mammal ever discovered, easily dwarfing modern elephants.
Characterized by a robust parietal-occipital cranial crest on its forehead that anchored massive neck muscles supporting its colossal head.
Coexisted with early hominins (such as archaic Homo / Narmada Man) throughout the Pleistocene of India.
Possessed nearly straight, massive upward-curving tusks that exceeded 3.5 meters in length.

sources.citation: Falconer, H., & Cautley, P. T. (1845). Fauna Antiqua Sivalensis, being the fossil zoology of the Sewalik Hills in the north of India.
Larramendi, A. (2016). Shoulder height, body mass, and shape of proboscideans. Acta Palaeontologica Polonica, 61(3), 537-574.

name: Tyrannotitan
dietDetails: Apex predator preying upon massive titanosaurian sauropods such as Patagotitan and Chubutisaurus.
sizeNotes: Massive carcharodontosaurid comparable in size to Giganotosaurus and Carcharodontosaurus, with heavily built dorsal vertebrae.
discoveryHistory: Found on the 'La Juanita' farm in Chubut in 1999 and formally described by Fernando Novas and colleagues in 2005.
interestingFacts: One of the earliest known giant carcharodontosaurids, predating both Giganotosaurus and Mapusaurus.
Unlike its later relatives, its teeth were less blade-like and bore wrinkly, undulating enamel surfaces adapted for crushing flesh.
Possessed extraordinarily short and stout arms, showing early evolutionary reduction in forelimb size among giganotosaurines.
Lived alongside giant titanosaur sauropods, which it attacked using slashing, wound-inflicting bites.

sources.citation: Novas, F. E., de Valais, S., Vickers-Rich, P., & Rich, T. (2005). A large Cretaceous theropod from Patagonia, Argentina, and the evolution of carcharodontosaurids. Naturwissenschaften, 92(5), 226-230.

name: Thalassodromeus
dietDetails: Terrestrial and aerial predator hunting small vertebrates, fish, squids, and lizards.
sizeNotes: Wingspan of approximately 4.2 to 4.5 meters; skull length of 1.4 meters, with the cranial crest accounting for 75% of skull surface area.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in calcium carbonate concretions in northeastern Brazil and described in 2002 by Alexander Kellner and Diogenes de Almeida Campos.
interestingFacts: Sported one of the largest cranial crests known relative to its skull, laced with extensive blood vessel impressions for thermoregulation and display.
Originally hypothesized to skim-feed, biomechanical studies later proved its neck and jaw could not withstand water resistance forces.
Operated as a terrestrial predator similar to modern storks, stalking small prey on the ground.
Its toothless, scissor-like jaws converged to a sharp tip capable of delivering powerful stabbing and slicing bites.

sources.citation: Kellner, A. W., & Campos, D. A. (2002). The function of the cranial crest and jaws of a unique pterosaur from the Early Cretaceous of Brazil. Science, 297(5580), 389-392.
Humphries, S., Bonser, R. H., Witton, M. P., & Martill, D. M. (2007). Did pterosaurs skim hunt? Did any of them? PLoS Biology, 5(8), e204.

name: Infernodrakon
dietDetails: Carnivorous azhdarchoid stalking small dinosaurs, mammals, amphibians, and reptiles on Cretaceous floodplains.
sizeNotes: Mid-sized azhdarchid with an estimated wingspan of approximately 4.5 to 5.0 meters.
discoveryHistory: Named and described based on holotype cervical and wing material recovered from the upper Hell Creek Formation of Montana.
interestingFacts: Coexisted directly with Tyrannosaurus rex, Triceratops, and the colossal giant pterosaur Quetzalcoatlus.
Demonstrates that medium-sized pterosaurs thrived alongside giant azhdarchids until the chicxulub asteroid impact.
Possessed elongated neck vertebrae and robust forelimbs adapted for efficient four-legged terrestrial stalking.
Features uniquely slender spear-like rostral morphology suggesting quick striking at small agile prey.

sources.citation: Longrich, N. R., Martill, D. M., & Andres, B. (2018). Late Maastrichtian pterosaurs confirm low extinction susceptibility prior to K-Pg. PLOS Biology, 16(3), e2001663.

name: Zhuchengtyrannus
dietDetails: Apex predator preying upon giant hadrosaurids like Shantungosaurus and large ceratopsians like Sinoceratops.
sizeNotes: One of the largest known tyrannosaurids, nearly matching Tyrannosaurus rex and Tarbosaurus in maxilla and dentary dimensions.
discoveryHistory: Found in 2009 during quarry excavations in Zhucheng and named by David Hone and colleagues in 2011.
interestingFacts: Shares anatomical features with Tarbosaurus but differs in having a distinctive horizontal shelf on the maxilla.
Hunted the colossal hadrosaur Shantungosaurus, one of the largest non-sauropod dinosaurs to ever walk the Earth.
Lived in a floodplain ecosystem characterized by catastrophic mass mortality events that preserved thousands of dinosaur bones.
Bore massive, bone-crushing jaws with deep rooted teeth designed to withstand extreme lateral biting forces.

sources.citation: Hone, D. W. E., Wang, K., Sullivan, C., et al. (2011). A new, large tyrannosaurine theropod from the Upper Cretaceous of China. Cretaceous Research, 32(4), 495-503.

name: Quinkana
dietDetails: Apex terrestrial predator hunting giant marsupials like Diprotodon, giant kangaroos (Procoptodon), and flightless birds.
sizeNotes: Ziphodont terrestrial crocodile with laterally compressed, recurved serrated teeth and an erect walking posture.
discoveryHistory: First described by Ralph Molnar in 1981 from Pliocene-Pleistocene cave and river deposits in northern Queensland.
interestingFacts: Unlike modern semi-aquatic crocodiles, Quinkana was fully terrestrial with upright legs capable of galloping pursuit.
Equipped with ziphodont teeth (laterally flattened and serrated like steak knives) designed for slicing mammal flesh.
One of Australia's apex predators alongside the giant monitor lizard Megalania and marsupial lion Thylacoleo.
Surviving until around 40,000 years ago, it encountered early indigenous Australians arriving on the continent.

sources.citation: Molnar, R. E. (1981). Pleistocene ziphodont crocodilians of Queensland. Records of the Australian Museum, 33(19), 803-834.

name: Haast's Eagle
dietDetails: Apex avian predator specialized in taking down giant flightless moa up to 15 times its own weight.
sizeNotes: Wingspan estimated at 2.6 to 3.0 meters; the largest eagle known to have existed, with talons matching those of a tiger.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in 1871 by F. Fuller at Glenmark and described by Julius von Haast as Harpagornis moorei (later reclassified into Hieraaetus by Bunce et al. 2005).
interestingFacts: Struck its prey with force equivalent to a concrete block falling from an eight-story building, crushing the pelvis of giant moa.
Possessed relatively short wings for its massive weight, adapted for maneuvering through dense southern beech forests.
Ancient Māori oral tradition remembers the eagle as the 'Pouākai', a terrifying man-eating raptor from the high mountains.
DNA analysis revealed its closest living relative is the tiny Little Eagle, demonstrating rapid evolutionary island gigantism.

sources.citation: Bunce, M., et al. (2005). Extreme reversed sexual size dimorphism in the extinct New Zealand eagle. PLoS Biology, 3(1), e9.

name: Zhejiangopterus
dietDetails: Terrestrial stalker feeding on small vertebrates, lizards, eggs, and invertebrates.
sizeNotes: Wingspan of approximately 3.5 meters; known from multiple well-preserved complete skeletons including juvenile and adult specimens.
discoveryHistory: Found in 1986 in Linhai County by a local quarry worker and described in 1994 by Cai Zhengquan and Wei Feng.
interestingFacts: One of the most anatomically complete azhdarchid pterosaurs ever discovered, providing critical data on azhdarchid neck structure.
Lacked the exaggerated cranial crests seen in many other pterosaurs, featuring a low, elongate, crestless skull with a sharp beak.
Its long neck vertebrae lacked cervical ribs, making the neck stiff and held upright like a modern stork.
Biomechanical analysis indicates it spent extensive time walking quadrupedally on land, picking off prey in open woodlands.

sources.citation: Cai, Z., & Wei, F. (1994). On a new pterosaur (Zhejiangopterus linhaiensis gen. et sp. nov.) from Upper Cretaceous in Linhai, Zhejiang, China. Vertebrata PalAsiatica, 32(3), 181-194.

name: Glyptodon
dietDetails: Low-browsing herbivore and grazer feeding on coarse grasses, roots, and riparian vegetation.
sizeNotes: Massive armadillo relative with a domed protective shell composed of more than 1,000 fused osteoderms.
discoveryHistory: First described by Sir Richard Owen in 1839 based on fossils collected in South America during Charles Darwin's voyage on HMS Beagle.
interestingFacts: Its rigid carapace was so strong and spacious that early indigenous humans in South America used empty shells as shelters.
The tail was encased in a series of flexible bony rings ending in a blunt sheath used for defense against predators like Smilodon.
Fused cervical and thoracic vertebrae formed a solid bony bridge to support the tremendous weight of its armor dome.
Survived until approximately 10,000 years ago, where hunting by early human populations contributed to its extinction.

sources.citation: Owen, R. (1839). Description of a tooth and part of the skeleton of the Glyptodon clavipes. Transactions of the Geological Society of London, 6, 81-106.

name: Thanatotheristes
nameMeaning: Reaper of death, honoring De Groots
dietDetails: Apex predator preying upon early ceratopsians like Xenoceratops and hadrosauroids.
sizeNotes: Oldest known tyrannosaurid from northern North America, with an adult skull measuring approximately 80 cm.
discoveryHistory: Found along the Bow River in Alberta in 2010 by local hikers John and Sandra De Groot, and described in 2020 by Jared Voris and colleagues.
interestingFacts: Nicknamed the 'Reaper of Death', it is the oldest named tyrannosaurid discovered in Canada, predating T. rex by about 12 million years.
Distinguished by a unique series of vertical ridges along the upper jaw margin (maxilla) in front of the eye socket.
Forms a distinct clade (Daspletosaurini) with Daspletosaurus, demonstrating that tyrannosaurids were ecologically partitioned into distinct lineages.
Deep, robust jaw construction indicates it delivered crushing bites to disable thick-skinned ceratopsian prey.

sources.citation: Voris, J. T., Therrien, F., Zelenitsky, D. K., & Brown, C. M. (2020). A new tyrannosaurine from the Canadian Late Cretaceous Foremost Formation. Cretaceous Research, 110, 104388.

name: Gigantspinosaurus
dietDetails: Low-browsing herbivore feeding on cycads, bennettitaleans, ferns, and horsetails in Jurassic river basins.
sizeNotes: Basal stegosaurian famous for its gargantuan shoulder spines, which were at least twice the length of its shoulder blades.
discoveryHistory: Uncovered in 1985 in Zigong, Sichuan, and formally described in 1992 by Ouyang Hui.
interestingFacts: Sported the largest shoulder spines (parascapular spines) of any known stegosaur, flaring backward over a meter in length.
In contrast to its giant shoulder spines, the paired plates running down its neck and back were remarkably small and rounded.
Considered a basal member of Stegosauria, preserving primitive traits transitional between early armored dinosaurs and derived stegosaurids.
Skin impressions discovered with the specimen revealed small, rounded, non-overlapping polygonal scales covering the body.

sources.citation: Ouyang, H. (1992). Discovery of Gigantspinosaurus sichuanensis and its scapular spine. Abstracts of the 5th Symposium of the Chinese Society of Vertebrate Paleontology, 47-49.

name: Gigantoraptor
dietDetails: Omnivore or herbivore consuming high foliage, seeds, tubers, and opportunistically small vertebrates with its robust beak.
sizeNotes: By far the largest known oviraptorosaurian, growing nearly 35 times heavier than most other oviraptorosaurs.
discoveryHistory: Accidentally unearthed in 2005 in front of a film crew filming a Japanese documentary on sauropod fossils; named in 2007 by Xu Xing et al.
interestingFacts: Reached a colossal size comparable to tyrannosaurids while retaining the light, bird-like skeletal features and toothless beak of oviraptorosaurs.
Bone histology of the holotype (LH V0011) revealed it was an 11-year-old subadult that was still actively growing at the time of death.
Despite weighing two tonnes, it had proportionally long, slender hind legs, indicating it was one of the fastest runners of its size.
Preserved pennaceous feathers on related oviraptorosaurs confirm that Gigantoraptor possessed feathered forelimbs used for brooding or display.

sources.citation: Xu, X., Tan, Q., Wang, J., Zhao, X., & Tan, L. (2007). A gigantic bird-like dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of China. Nature, 447(7146), 841-844.

name: Rinchenia
dietDetails: Omnivore feeding on seeds, nuts, foliage, eggs, mollusks, and small vertebrates in Cretaceous river floodplains.
sizeNotes: Known from holotype MPC-D 100/32A, featuring a remarkably tall, thin, dome-like cranial crest.
discoveryHistory: Found in 1984 in the Nemegt Basin; originally described by Rinchen Barsbold as Oviraptor mongoliensis, and placed in its own genus Rinchenia in 1997 by Halszka Osmólska.
interestingFacts: Possessed a dramatically tall, bulbous casque-like skull crest made of delicate porous bone, resembling that of a modern cassowary.
The crest served primarily as a visual display structure for species recognition and sexual selection in the lush Nemegt environment.
Equipped with an exceptionally robust, short lower jaw and toothless keratinous beak capable of cracking hard plant seeds and shellfish.
Its fused tail vertebrae (pygostyle) supported a fan of plumage used in mating displays.

sources.citation: Barsbold, R. (1986). Raubdinosaurier Oviraptoren. In: Vorobyeva, E. I. (ed.), Gerpetologicheskie Issledovaniya v Mongolskoy Narodnoy Respublike, 210-223.

name: Coelurosauravus
nameMeaning: Grandfather of hollow lizards of Eliva
dietDetails: Insectivore hunting arboreal insects, early cockroaches, and arthropods within Permian conifer canopies.
sizeNotes: Slender gliding diapsid reptile with a body length of around 40 cm and a delicate wing membrane.
discoveryHistory: First described by French paleontologist Jean Piveteau in 1926 based on a fossil discovered in Madagascar.
interestingFacts: The earliest known gliding vertebrate in the fossil record, predating gliding dinosaurs and pterosaurs by tens of millions of years.
Unlike modern flying lizards whose wings are supported by ribs, Coelurosauravus sprouted specialized bony rods completely separate from the rib cage.
Possessed a heavily serrated parietal crest on the back of its skull adorned with pointed spines, resembling modern horned chameleons.
Equipped with curved, sharp claws well suited for gripping and scrambling vertically along ancient tree bark.

sources.citation: Piveteau, J. (1926). Paléontologie de Madagascar. XIII. Amphibiens et reptiles permiens. Annales de Paléontologie, 15, 53-179.
Frey, E., Sues, H.-D., & Munk, W. (1997). Gliding mechanism in the Late Permian reptile Coelurosauravus. Science, 275(5305), 1450-1452.

name: Linhenykus
dietDetails: Specialized insectivore using its single stout thumb claw to dig into subterranean ant and termite mounds.
sizeNotes: Tiny alvarezsaurid weighing under half a kilogram, famous for having only one functional digit on each hand.
discoveryHistory: Found in 2008 in red sandstone beds at Bayan Mandahu by Jonah Choiniere and Michael Pittman, and described in 2011 by Xu Xing et al.
interestingFacts: The only known non-avian dinosaur to possess just a single functional finger (a stout clawed thumb) on each forelimb.
The second and third fingers were entirely absent or reduced to vestigial specks of bone, representing the extreme endpoint of theropod arm reduction.
Like modern pangolins and anteaters, its hyper-specialized single claws were adapted for ripping into hardened insect nests.
Had long, gracile bird-like hind legs capable of rapid running across arid desert dunes.

sources.citation: Xu, X., Sullivan, C., Pittman, M., et al. (2011). A monodactyl nonavian dinosaur and the complex evolution of the alvarezsauroid hand. PNAS, 108(6), 2338-2342.

name: Stomatosuchus
dietDetails: Piscivore and filter feeder straining small fish, crustaceans, and plankton using an expandable pelican-like throat pouch.
sizeNotes: Giant crocodile with a flattened, shovel-shaped skull nearly 2 meters long, featuring a completely toothless lower jaw.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in 1911 by Ernst Stromer in the Bahariya Oasis, Egypt, and described in 1925; tragically, the sole holotype skull was destroyed during an Allied bombing raid on Munich in 1944.
interestingFacts: Possessed an entirely toothless lower jaw paired with only tiny conical teeth in the upper jaw, unique among giant crocodylomorphs.
Believed to have possessed a massive, flexible gular throat pouch like a pelican to trap shoals of freshwater fish.
The only known fossil specimen was destroyed when the Alte Akademie museum in Munich was bombed during World War II.
Coexisted in North Africa's mangrove swamps with Spinosaurus and Carcharodontosaurus.

sources.citation: Stromer, E. (1925). Ergebnisse der Forschungsreisen Prof. E. Stromers in den Wüsten Ägyptens. 7. Stomatosuchus inermis Stromer. Abhandlungen der Bayerischen Akademie der Wissenschaften.

name: Kariridraco
dietDetails: Frugivore and opportunistic omnivore feeding on gymnosperm fruits, seeds, and small vertebrates in coastal forests.
sizeNotes: Tapejarid pterosaur with a well-preserved skull and jaws exhibiting an estimated wingspan of approximately 2.5 meters.
discoveryHistory: Named and described in 2021 by Gabriela Cerqueira and colleagues from a well-preserved skull excavated in northeastern Brazil.
interestingFacts: Distinguished by a sharp, deep sagittal cranial crest that curved downward along the premaxilla at a unique 45-degree angle.
Features unusually deep premaxillary margins and short, toothless, downturned jaws specialized for harvesting hard prehistoric fruits.
Named in honor of both the indigenous Kariri ethnic nation and the comic book heroine Diana Prince (Wonder Woman).
Belongs to the Tapejarinae, an endemic clade of ornate-crested pterosaurs that diversified rapidly across Gondwana.

sources.citation: Cerqueira, G. M., Santos, M. A., Marks, M. F., Sayão, J. M., & Pinheiro, F. L. (2021). A new tapejarine pterosaur from the Upper Cretaceous of Brazil. Historical Biology, 34(5), 875-885.

name: Megabalaena
dietDetails: Bulk filter-feeder swallowing dense swarms of euphausiids (krill), copepods, and small schooling fish.

media.credit: Y. Tanaka, T. Kimura, T. Shinmura, H. Ohira & H. Furusawa (CC BY 4.0)

sizeNotes: Early giant true right whale (Balaenidae) reaching lengths comparable to modern northern right whales.
discoveryHistory: Found in 2004 along the riverbed of the Aoki River in Nagano, Japan, and described in 2024 by Yoshihiro Tanaka and colleagues.
interestingFacts: Represents one of the earliest occurrences of gigantism among true right whales, demonstrating gigantism evolved earlier than previously thought.
Possessed a strongly arched rostrum and deep lower jaw specifically adapted to house very long baleen plates.
Unlike most modern right whales restricted to cold polar seas, Megabalaena inhabited warm temperate coastal waters in the Miocene Pacific.
Well-preserved auditory bulla and skull bones provide crucial evolutionary clues linking archaic cetotheres to living right whales.

sources.citation: Tanaka, Y., Kimura, T., Shinmura, T., Ohira, H., & Furusawa, H. (2024). A new late Miocene right whale (Balaenidae) from Japan and the evolution of body size in baleen whales. Journal of Systematic Palaeontology, 22(1), 2321453.

name: Scylacosaurus
dietDetails: Active carnivorous predator preying on small dicynodonts, parareptiles, and early archosauromorphs.
sizeNotes: Medium-sized basal therocephalian with a long, slender snout and prominent canine tusks.
discoveryHistory: First described by famed South African paleontologist Robert Broom in 1903 from Karoo Basin deposits near Colesberg.
interestingFacts: Equipped with prominent mammalian-style canine fangs and sharp postcanine teeth, reflecting the transition toward mammal-like carnivory.
Possessed deep grooves on its maxillary bones that some researchers hypothesize may have housed early venom delivery glands.
Endocranial casts indicate it had an acute sense of smell and whisker pits on the snout indicating tactile facial hair.
Thrived across southern Gondwana shortly before the devastating Permian-Triassic extinction event.

sources.citation: Broom, R. (1903). On some new primitive theriodonts in the South African Museum. Annals of the South African Museum, 4, 147-158.

name: Apolithabatis
dietDetails: Benthic feeder preying on crustaceans, mollusks, bivalves, and small reef fish in shallow Tethys lagoons.

media.credit: J. Türtscher, P. L. Jambura, F. Spindler & J. Kriwet (CC BY 4.0)

sizeNotes: Disc width of approximately 75 cm with an elongated whip-like tail bearing a serrated defensive spine.
discoveryHistory: Named and described in 2024 by Julia Türtscher and an international team of paleoichthyologists from exceptionally preserved Monte Bolca fossils.
interestingFacts: Preserved in the world-famous Monte Bolca Lagerstätte with complete mineralized cartilage, tooth pavement plates, and skin outlines intact.
Equipped with flattened crushing dental plates arranged in pavement patterns, designed to crush thick-shelled crabs and gastropods.
Inhabited the tropical coral reef atolls of the western Tethys Ocean during the early Eocene thermal optimum.
Demonstrates that modern eagle ray swimming dynamics and reef foraging adaptations were already fully established 50 million years ago.

sources.citation: Türtscher, J., Jambura, P. L., Spindler, F., & Kriwet, J. (2024). Morphological and phylogenetic revision of batoid fishes from the Eocene of Monte Bolca, Italy. Journal of Paleontology.

name: Jormungandr
dietDetails: Apex marine predator preying on cephalopods, hesperornithiform diving birds, sea turtles, and bony fish.
sizeNotes: Transitional mosasaur exhibiting an intermediate mosaic of primitive Clidastes-like and advanced Mosasaurus-like cranial traits.
discoveryHistory: Found in 2015 along the Pembina River in Cavalier County, North Dakota, and described in 2023 by Amelia Zietlow, Clint Boyd, and Mark Norell.
interestingFacts: Represents a crucial 'missing link' mosasaur documenting how plioplatecarpines transitioned into apex giants like Mosasaurus.
Retained primitive characteristics including 11 ribs above the pelvis while evolving advanced, crushing jaw morphology.
Inhabited the frigid, nutrient-rich waters of the Western Interior Seaway which split North America in half.
Its fossil skull preserves distinct rugose brow ridges above the eye sockets that may have supported protective structures.

sources.citation: Zietlow, A. R., Boyd, C. A., & Norell, M. A. (2023). Jormungandr walhallaensis, a new mosasaurine from the Late Cretaceous of North Dakota. Bulletin of the American Museum of Natural History, 464, 1-108.

name: Plotosaurus
dietDetails: High-speed pursuit predator hunting fast-swimming pelagic fish, belemnites, and ammonites in the open Pacific Ocean.

geographicRange.region: Fresno County & San Joaquin Valley, California

sizeNotes: The most hydrodynamically advanced mosasaur known, sporting narrow, streamlined flippers and a stiffened, carangiform torso.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in 1937 by high school student Allan Bennison in the Panoche Hills of California, and named by Charles Lewis Camp in 1942.
interestingFacts: The pinnacle of mosasaur hydrodynamic evolution: possessed a stiff, streamlined fusiform body resembling an ichthyosaur or tuna.
Unlike serpentine mosasaurs that undulated their entire bodies, Plotosaurus swam using carangiform locomotion powered strictly by a crescent-shaped tail fin.
Skin impressions revealed tiny, tightly packed keeled scales that significantly reduced water friction during high-speed chases.
Large eyes equipped with sclerotic rings allowed it to hunt in deep, dimly lit offshore Pacific waters.
